claim: MDCK cells stably transfected with YFP-tagged keratin 8 show comparable amounts of YFP-tagged and endogenous keratin 8.
source: Immunoblot analysis of total cell lysates revealed comparable amounts of YFP-tagged and endogenous keratin 8 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: MDCK cells form a one-layered coherent epithelium with cuboidal to cylindrical cells attached to each other by highly organized junctional complexes.
source: MDCK cells form a one-layered coherent epithelium with the cuboidal to cylindrical cells attached to each other by highly organized junctional complexes.
evidence: Stated as a known characteristic of MDCK cells

claim: MDCK cells have a complex keratin filament arrangement consisting of a dense subapical network, perinuclear and radial keratin filaments, and interdesmosomal filaments below the plasma membrane.
source: Intracellularly, the keratin filaments have a complex arrangement consisting of a dense subapical network, perinuclear and radial keratin filaments, and interdesmosomal filaments below the plasma membrane (Quinlan et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Quinlan et al., 2017

claim: HaCaT cells contain pancytoplasmic keratin filament networks whose 3D organization is only partially elucidated.
source: They contain pancytoplasmic keratin filament networks whose 3D organization is only partially elucidated (Moch et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Moch et al., 2020

claim: The keratin 8-YFP knock-in mouse line expresses only YFP-tagged keratin 8 but no wild-type keratin 8.
source: To examine the 3D organization of the keratin intermediate filament network in its native tissue context, we made use of the recently described knock-in mouse line expressing only YFP-tagged keratin 8 but no wild-type keratin 8.
evidence: Stated as a characteristic of the mouse model used

claim: Visual inspection showed a high degree of overlap between the recorded fluorescence and the derived numerical positions of vertices at all subcellular locations.
source: Visual inspection showed a high degree of overlap between the recorded fluorescence and the derived numerical positions of vertices (dotted lines) at all subcellular locations.
evidence: Based on visual comparison of fluorescence images and segmentation results

claim: TSOAX can be used to reliably segment keratin networks in entire cells.
source: We now show that TSOAX can be used to reliably segment keratin networks in entire cells.
evidence: Demonstrated through application of TSOAX to keratin network images

claim: An apical and a basal keratin filament network domain can be distinguished in MDCK cells.
source: Thus, an apical and a basal keratin filament network domain can be distinguished in MDCK cells (Video 2).
evidence: Observed in 3D renderings shown in Video 2

claim: The major difference between apical and basal domains in MDCK cells are the thicker keratin bundles in the basal domain.
source: The major difference between both domains are the thicker keratin bundles in the basal domain.
evidence: Observed from analysis of keratin network renderings

claim: HaCaT cells are extremely flat and do not show a clearly separated apical and basal network and lack a distinct lateral network.
source: HaCaT cells are extremly flat and do not show a clearly seperated apical and basal network and lack a distinct lateral network (Video 3).
evidence: Observed in 3D renderings shown in Video 3

claim: A prominent feature of HaCaT cells' keratin filament network are long filament bundles that often run in parallel.
source: A prominent feature of their keratin filament network are long filament bundles that often run in parallel.
evidence: Observed from analysis of HaCaT cell keratin networks

claim: The keratin network is less dense in RPE cells than in the other two cell types.
source: The keratin network is less dense in RPE cells than in the other two cell types (Video 4).
evidence: Observed in 3D renderings shown in Video 4

claim: In RPE cells, the perinuclear network contains thicker filaments at the apical than the basal side.
source: In contrast to MDCK cells, the perinuclear network contains thicker filaments at the apical than the basal side.
evidence: Observed from analysis of RPE cell keratin networks

claim: Filament segments with a medium brightness dominated in MDCK cells with a near Gaussian distribution.
source: The quantifications show that filament segments with a medium brightness dominated in MDCK cells with a near Gaussian distribution, whereas thin filaments were prevalent in HaCaT and RPE cells.
evidence: Shown in histograms in Figure 3A-C

claim: Thin filaments were prevalent in HaCaT and RPE cells.
source: The quantifications show that filament segments with a medium brightness dominated in MDCK cells with a near Gaussian distribution, whereas thin filaments were prevalent in HaCaT and RPE cells.
evidence: Shown in histograms in Figure 3A-C

claim: Thin filaments were most abundant in HaCaT cells.
source: Thin filaments were most abundant in HaCaT cells.
evidence: Shown in histograms in Figure 3A-C

claim: Thin filaments were numerous in the cell periphery in each cell type.
source: In each case, thin filaments were numerous in the cell periphery.
evidence: Observed in brightness maps shown in Figure 3D-F

claim: Increased de novo single filament formation occurs in the cell periphery.
source: This may be due to the increased de novo single filament formation in these regions (Windoffer et al., 2004; Windoffer et al., 2006, Moch et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work

claim: Significantly more segments were detected in HaCaT cells than in the other cell types.
source: Significantly more segments were detected in HaCaT cells than in the other cell types (Figure 4A).
evidence: Shown in quantitative analysis in Figure 4A

claim: The average segment length was shortest in MDCK cells (0.80 ± 0.04 µm).
source: The average segment length was shortest in MDCK cells (0.80 ± 0.04 µm), longest in RPE cells (0.88 ± 0.05 µm) and intermediate in HaCaT cells (0.83 ± 0.13 µm) (Figure 4B).
evidence: Measured from segmented networks and shown in Figure 4B

claim: The average segment length was longest in RPE cells (0.88 ± 0.05 µm).
source: The average segment length was shortest in MDCK cells (0.80 ± 0.04 µm), longest in RPE cells (0.88 ± 0.05 µm) and intermediate in HaCaT cells (0.83 ± 0.13 µm) (Figure 4B).
evidence: Measured from segmented networks and shown in Figure 4B

claim: The average segment length was intermediate in HaCaT cells (0.83 ± 0.13 µm).
source: The average segment length was shortest in MDCK cells (0.80 ± 0.04 µm), longest in RPE cells (0.88 ± 0.05 µm) and intermediate in HaCaT cells (0.83 ± 0.13 µm) (Figure 4B).
evidence: Measured from segmented networks and shown in Figure 4B

claim: The combined length of all segments per cell was similar in MDCK (1.63 ± 0.41 mm) and RPE cells (1.57 ± 0.48 mm).
source: The combined length of all segments per cell (Figure 4C) was similar in MDCK (1.63 ± 0.41 mm) and RPE cells (1.57 ± 0.48 mm) but was more than twice longer in HaCaT cells (4.40 ± 1.53 mm).
evidence: Measured from segmented networks and shown in Figure 4C

claim: The combined length of all segments per cell was more than twice longer in HaCaT cells (4.40 ± 1.53 mm) than in MDCK and RPE cells.
source: The combined length of all segments per cell (Figure 4C) was similar in MDCK (1.63 ± 0.41 mm) and RPE cells (1.57 ± 0.48 mm) but was more than twice longer in HaCaT cells (4.40 ± 1.53 mm).
evidence: Measured from segmented networks and shown in Figure 4C

claim: Cell volumes were 4.65 ± 1.13 µm³ for MDCK, 9.16 ± 6.10 µm³ for HaCaT and 2.73 ± 0.95 µm³ for RPE.
source: Significant differences could be detected, i.e., 4.65 ± 1.13 µm³ for MDCK, 9.16 ± 6.10 µm³ for HaCaT and 2.73 ± 0.95 µm³ for RPE (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Measured from image data and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A

claim: Filament density was comparable in HaCaT (604.82 ± 304.20 µm/µm³) and RPE cells (585.60 ± 63.97 µm/µm³).
source: Taking the different cell volumes into account, filament density, that is filament length per volume, was comparable in HaCaT (604.82 ± 304.20 µm/µm³) and RPE cells (585.60 ± 63.97 µm/µm³), while it was considerably lower in MDCK cells (355.24 ± 56.49 µm/µm³) (Figure 4D).
evidence: Calculated from filament length and cell volume data, shown in Figure 4D

claim: Filament density was considerably lower in MDCK cells (355.24 ± 56.49 µm/µm³) than in HaCaT and RPE cells.
source: Taking the different cell volumes into account, filament density, that is filament length per volume, was comparable in HaCaT (604.82 ± 304.20 µm/µm³) and RPE cells (585.60 ± 63.97 µm/µm³), while it was considerably lower in MDCK cells (355.24 ± 56.49 µm/µm³) (Figure 4D).
evidence: Calculated from filament length and cell volume data, shown in Figure 4D

claim: The entire length of epidermal keratin filament bundles in an individual human should be ~600,000 km.
source: Given that the human body has ~0.14 x 1012 epidermal cells (Bianconi et al., 2013), the entire length of epidermal keratin filament bundles in an individual should be ~600,000 km.
evidence: Calculated from measured filament length per cell and estimated number of epidermal cells

claim: There are ~1.14 × 10^7 km of single keratin filaments in the epidermis of a human body.
source: Assuming a bundling rate of 19 filaments per filament bundle (Hémonnot et al., 2016) there are ~1.14 × 107 km of single keratin filaments in the epidermis of a human body.
evidence: Calculated from total bundle length and bundling factor from literature

claim: The amount of keratin per HaCaT cell is 3.47 pg.
source: By using the following formula ((MPL * Ltot * Bf) / Na) [Na = Avogadro constant], the amount of keratin per cell is 3.47 pg.
evidence: Calculated from measured filament length, mass per length, and bundling factor

claim: An alternative estimate of keratin content in HaCaT cells is ~4.3 pg/cell.
source: Assuming a bundling factor of 19 and a total keratin filament bundle length of ~4.4 mm in HaCaT keratinocytes, the total MW of keratin/cell is 2,60E+12 Da corresponding to a mass of ~4.3 pg/cell.
evidence: Calculated from tetrameric subunit dimensions and total filament length

claim: The keratin content per MDCK cell is 1.3 pg or 1.4 pg.
source: Performing the same type of calculation we deduced a keratin content of 1.3 pg or 1.4 pg per MDCK cell and 1.2 pg or 1.4 pg for single RPE cells.
evidence: Calculated using the same methods as for HaCaT cells

claim: The keratin content per RPE cell is 1.2 pg or 1.4 pg.
source: Performing the same type of calculation we deduced a keratin content of 1.3 pg or 1.4 pg per MDCK cell and 1.2 pg or 1.4 pg for single RPE cells.
evidence: Calculated using the same methods as for HaCaT cells

claim: The Y-shaped organization (three segments per node) was by far the most frequent configuration (~60%).
source: Our analyses show that the Y-shaped organization (three segments per node) was by far the most frequent configuration (~60%) followed by the X-shaped (four segment per node) arrangement (~30%) and rarely higher degrees of branching (~10%) (Figure 5).
evidence: Quantified from segmented networks and shown in Figure 5

claim: The X-shaped (four segment per node) arrangement was the second most frequent configuration (~30%).
source: Our analyses show that the Y-shaped organization (three segments per node) was by far the most frequent configuration (~60%) followed by the X-shaped (four segment per node) arrangement (~30%) and rarely higher degrees of branching (~10%) (Figure 5).
evidence: Quantified from segmented networks and shown in Figure 5

claim: Higher degrees of branching (more than 4 segments per node) occur rarely (~10%).
source: Our analyses show that the Y-shaped organization (three segments per node) was by far the most frequent configuration (~60%) followed by the X-shaped (four segment per node) arrangement (~30%) and rarely higher degrees of branching (~10%) (Figure 5).
evidence: Quantified from segmented networks and shown in Figure 5

claim: The highest distance/length ratios were observed in MDCK (0.92 ± 0.09) and HaCaT (0.92 ± 0.08).
source: The highest ratios were observed in MDCK (0.92 ± 0.09) and HaCaT (0.92 ± 0.08), which were significantly higher than in RPE cells (0.90 ± 0.10) indicating that the filaments in RPE cells are less straight.
evidence: Calculated from segmented networks and shown in Figure 6A

claim: The distance/length ratio in RPE cells (0.90 ± 0.10) was significantly lower than in MDCK and HaCaT cells, indicating that filaments in RPE cells are less straight.
source: The highest ratios were observed in MDCK (0.92 ± 0.09) and HaCaT (0.92 ± 0.08), which were significantly higher than in RPE cells (0.90 ± 0.10) indicating that the filaments in RPE cells are less straight.
evidence: Calculated from segmented networks and shown in Figure 6A

claim: There is no correlation between filament bundle thickness and curvature.
source: We did not see a correlation between filament bundle thickness and curvature (pairwise Pearson correlation coefficient in MDCK = –0.10, HaCaT = 0.08, RPE = 0.14).
evidence: Calculated Pearson correlation coefficients from measured data

claim: The calculated persistence length values (~2.6 µm) do not differ significantly between the three cell types.
source: Figure 4—figure supplement 1B shows that the calculated values (~2.6 µm) do not differ significantly between the three cell types.
evidence: Calculated from segmented networks and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B

claim: The calculated persistence length (~2.6 µm) is higher than the experimentally determined persistence length of single filaments.
source: As expected, they are higher than the experimentally determined persistence length of single filaments (cf. Block et al., 2015).
evidence: Comparison with literature values from Block et al., 2015

claim: The azimuth distribution is quite even in MDCK and RPE cells but not in HaCaT cells.
source: Comparing the determined values with the expected values for segments orientated evenly in all directions, shows that the azimuth distribution is quite even in MDCK and RPE cells but not in HaCat cells.
evidence: Shown in histograms in Figure 7A-C

claim: All cells have an uneven distribution of vertical orientation, indicating that segments are preferentially oriented horizontally.
source: All cells have an uneven distribution of vertical orientation, indicating that segments are preferentially oriented horizontally.
evidence: Shown in histograms in Figure 7D-F

claim: The azimuth distribution in HaCaT is more oriented than in MDCK or RPE cells.
source: Compilations of the analyses for all cells (Figure 7G and H) confirmed the single-cell data and affirmed that the azimuth distribution in HaCaT is more oriented than in MDCK or RPE cells.
evidence: Shown in quantitative analysis in Figure 7G

claim: The elevation orientation is more directed in MDCK and HaCaT cells than in RPE cells.
source: Furthermore, the elevation orientation is more directed in MDCK and HaCaT cells than in RPE cells.
evidence: Shown in quantitative analysis in Figure 7H

claim: MDCK and RPE cells showed a homogenous distribution of horizontal segment orientation in the x/y plane while HaCaT cells were more polarized.
source: As expected, MDCK and RPE cells showed a homogenous distribution of horizontal segment orientation in the x/y plane while HaCaT cells were more polarized (Figure 8A–C).
evidence: Shown in radial histograms in Figure 8A-C

claim: In the vertical direction (y/z plane), horizontally oriented segments predominate in MDCK and HaCaT cells while segments are more uniformly oriented in RPE cells.
source: In the vertical direction (y/z plane), horizontally oriented segments predominate in MDCK and HaCaT cells while segments are more uniformly oriented in RPE cells (Figure 8D–F).
evidence: Shown in radial histograms in Figure 8D-F

claim: The sum vectors in MDCK and RPE cells are relatively small, indicating an isotropic orientation of the respective keratin networks.
source: The sum vectors in MDCK and RPE cells are relatively small, indicating an isotropic orientation of the respective keratin networks.
evidence: Calculated from segment orientation data and shown in Figure 8G-I

claim: The sum vectors in HaCaT cells are much longer than in MDCK and RPE cells, indicating a higher degree of anisotropy of the keratin network.
source: In contrast, the sum vectors in HaCaT cells are much longer, indicating a higher degree of anisotropy of the keratin network (Figure 8K).
evidence: Calculated from segment orientation data and shown in Figure 8K

claim: Keratin filaments are highly flexible and extensible.
source: Keratin filaments are highly flexible and extensible (Block et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Block et al., 2015

claim: Keratin filaments form hollow tubes with remarkable variability in local diameter and ultrastructure.
source: They form hollow tubes with remarkable variability in local diameter and ultrastructure (Weber et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Weber et al., 2021

claim: Keratin filaments generate branched bundles of different thickness forming anisotropic networks.
source: Keratin filaments generate branched bundles of different thickness forming anisotropic networks (Beil et al., 2005; Martin et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Beil et al., 2005 and Martin et al., 2016

claim: Network organization is affected by mechanical stress.
source: Network organization is furthermore affected by mechanical stress (Beriault et al., 2012; Felder et al., 2008; Fois et al., 2013; Karsch et al., 2020; Lutz et al., 2020; Quinlan et al., 2017) and differentiation-status (Coch and Leube, 2016; Iwatsuki and Suda, 2010; Leube et al., 2017; Quinlan et al., 2017; Tateishi et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Network organization is affected by differentiation status.
source: Network organization is furthermore affected by mechanical stress (Beriault et al., 2012; Felder et al., 2008; Fois et al., 2013; Karsch et al., 2020; Lutz et al., 2020; Quinlan et al., 2017) and differentiation-status (Coch and Leube, 2016; Iwatsuki and Suda, 2010; Leube et al., 2017; Quinlan et al., 2017; Tateishi et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Individual proteins such as Ndel1 and plectin regulate keratin network organization.
source: In addition, individual proteins such as Ndel1 and plectin have been shown to regulate keratin network organization (Kim et al., 2021; Moch et al., 2016; Osmanagic-Myers et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kim et al., 2021; Moch et al., 2016; Osmanagic-Myers et al., 2006

claim: TSOAX is an implementation of SOAX.
source: It is an implementation of SOAX (Xu et al., 2015; Xu et al., 2011), which was developed from the Stretching Open Active Contours (SOAC) algorithm (Li et al., 2010; Li et al., 2009).
evidence: Stated as a fact about the software with supporting citations

claim: SOAX was developed from the Stretching Open Active Contours (SOAC) algorithm.
source: It is an implementation of SOAX (Xu et al., 2015; Xu et al., 2011), which was developed from the Stretching Open Active Contours (SOAC) algorithm (Li et al., 2010; Li et al., 2009).
evidence: Stated as a fact about the software with supporting citations

claim: TSOAX has been applied for 3D segmentation of actin networks using fluorescence images of yeast cells.
source: TSOAX has been applied for 3D segmentation of actin networks using fluorescence images of yeast cells (Xu et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Xu et al., 2019

claim: The human genome contains 54 keratin genes.
source: The human genome contains 54 keratin genes, which are expressed in epithelia and epidermal appendages in a cell type-specific pattern (Jacob et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jacob et al., 2018

claim: Keratin genes are expressed in epithelia and epidermal appendages in a cell type-specific pattern.
source: The human genome contains 54 keratin genes, which are expressed in epithelia and epidermal appendages in a cell type-specific pattern (Jacob et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jacob et al., 2018

claim: Keratin filaments confer mechanical resilience together with their associated desmosomal cell-cell and hemidesmosomal cell-extracellular matrix adhesions.
source: They confer, together with their associated desmosomal cell-cell and hemidesmosomal cell-extracellular matrix adhesions, mechanical resilience (Hatzfeld et al., 2017; Te Molder et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hatzfeld et al., 2017 and Te Molder et al., 2021

claim: The calculated persistence length (~2.6 µm) is low in comparison to actin filaments (~10 µm) and microtubules (~5000 µm).
source: This is low in comparison to actin filaments (~10 µm) (De La Cruz and Gardel, 2015; Isambert et al., 1995; Takatsuki et al., 2014) and microtubules (~5000 µm) (Hawkins et al., 2010).
evidence: Comparison with literature values for other cytoskeletal filaments

claim: Keratin intermediate filaments can be extended under tension forming straight filaments and buckle under compression.
source: Keratin intermediate filaments are highly elastic (Kreplak et al., 2005; Wagner et al., 2007; Yamada et al., 2003). They can be extended under tension forming straight filaments and buckle under compression ( = negative tension) (Fudge et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: Straight segments were almost completely absent in all cells suggesting overall negative tension of the keratin networks.
source: Straight segments were almost completely absent in all cells suggesting overall negative tension of the keratin networks.
evidence: Observed from curvature measurements and inferred based on mechanical properties

claim: The 10 nm filaments are only loosely connected in keratin bundles.
source: The observation that filament bundle thickness and curvature are not correlated suggests that the 10 nm filaments are only loosely connected in keratin bundles.
evidence: Inferred from lack of correlation between thickness and curvature

claim: Uniformly radial orientation of keratin filament segments indicates that cells experience mechanical forces that are homogenous in all directions.
source: We suggest that uniformly radial orientation of keratin filament segments indicates that cells experience mechanical forces that are homogenous in all directions.
evidence: Proposed interpretation of orientation data

claim: A preferential orientation in one direction indicates that keratin filaments align in response to mechanical cues that may be induced by unevenly distributed cell-cell contacts, polarized cell-extracellular matrix adhesions or contractile activity.
source: In contrast, a preferential orientation in one direction indicates that keratin filaments align in response to mechanical cues that may be induced by unevenly distributed cell-cell contacts, polarized cell-extracellular matrix adhesions or contractile activity.
evidence: Proposed interpretation of orientation data

claim: HaCaT cells are subjected to mechanical strain.
source: Our data therefore indicate that HaCaT cells are subjected to mechanical strain (uneven azimuth distribution and large sum vector), whereas MDCK and RPE are subjected to little mechanical strain (uniform azimuth distribution and small sum vector).
evidence: Inferred from orientation measurements

claim: MDCK and RPE cells are subjected to little mechanical strain.
source: Our data therefore indicate that HaCaT cells are subjected to mechanical strain (uneven azimuth distribution and large sum vector), whereas MDCK and RPE are subjected to little mechanical strain (uniform azimuth distribution and small sum vector).
evidence: Inferred from orientation measurements

claim: The variation in filament bundling in the different cell types may be a consequence of differences in the local force balance.
source: The observed variation in filament bundling in the different cell types may therefore be a consequence of differences in the local force balance.
evidence: Proposed interpretation of brightness/bundling data

claim: The variation in filament thickness may reflect the propensity of the network to reorganize, for example, at different times of the cell cycle.
source: However, the variation in filament thickness may also reflect other properties such as the propensity of the network to reorganize, for example, at different times of the cell cycle.
evidence: Proposed alternative interpretation of thickness variation

claim: Mesh size may be determined by intrinsic keratin filament properties such as elastic modulus or branching capacity.
source: A conclusion of this observation is that mesh size may be determined by intrinsic keratin filament properties such as elastic modulus or branching capacity.
evidence: Proposed interpretation of segment length data

claim: A self-regulatory mechanism may control the balance between enlargement and reduction of individual meshes.
source: A self-regulatory mechanism may thus control the balance between enlargement and reduction of individual meshes.
evidence: Proposed mechanism based on observed mesh dynamics

claim: The Y-shaped joining of three segments may be linked to the bundling mechanism involving electrostatic and hydrophobic interactions.
source: The Y-shaped joining of three segments may be linked to the recently proposed bundling mechanism involving electrostatic and hydrophobic interactions (Haimov et al., 2020).
evidence: Proposed interpretation based on citation to Haimov et al., 2020

claim: The X-shaped intersections may be related to the disulfide-bond-mediated interactions reported for keratins 5/14.
source: On the other hand, the X-shaped intersections may be related to the disulfide-bond-mediated interactions reported for keratins 5/14 (Lee et al., 2012).
evidence: Proposed interpretation based on citation to Lee et al., 2012

claim: Preventing disulfide-bond-mediated links resulted in altered keratin filament network dynamics and epidermal tissue homeostasis.
source: In this instance, preventing these links resulted in altered keratin filament network dynamics and epidermal tissue homeostasis (Feng and Coulombe, 2015; Guo et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Feng and Coulombe, 2015 and Guo et al., 2020

claim: Experimental and mechanistic evidence has been provided for keratin filament branching.
source: Experimental and mechanistic evidence has been provided for keratin filament branching (Beil et al., 2005; Feng and Coulombe, 2015; Lee et al., 2012; Martin et al., 2016; Nafeey et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: The human body has ~0.14 x 10^12 epidermal cells.
source: Given that the human body has ~0.14 x 1012 epidermal cells (Bianconi et al., 2013), the entire length of epidermal keratin filament bundles in an individual should be ~600,000 km.
evidence: Supported by citation to Bianconi et al., 2013

claim: The mass per length of keratin filaments is 25 kDa/nm (range: 19–30 kDa/nm).
source: To this end, we take the experimentally determined mass per length (MPL) of keratin filaments of 25 kDa/nm (range: 19–30 kDa/nm; Herrmann et al., 1999) and a bundling factor (Bf) of 19 (Hémonnot et al., 2016) into account.
evidence: Supported by citation to Herrmann et al., 1999

claim: The bundling factor of keratin filaments is 19.
source: To this end, we take the experimentally determined mass per length (MPL) of keratin filaments of 25 kDa/nm (range: 19–30 kDa/nm; Herrmann et al., 1999) and a bundling factor (Bf) of 19 (Hémonnot et al., 2016) into account.
evidence: Supported by citation to Hémonnot et al., 2016

claim: A keratin tetramer has a length of 44 nm.
source: A keratin tetramer has a length of 44 nm (Parry et al., 2007) and consists primarily of two keratin 5 and two keratin 14 polypeptides with a combined molecular weight of 228 165 Da in keratinocytes.
evidence: Supported by citation to Parry et al., 2007

claim: A keratin tetramer consists primarily of two keratin 5 and two keratin 14 polypeptides with a combined molecular weight of 228,165 Da in keratinocytes.
source: A keratin tetramer has a length of 44 nm (Parry et al., 2007) and consists primarily of two keratin 5 and two keratin 14 polypeptides with a combined molecular weight of 228 165 Da in keratinocytes.
evidence: Stated as a fact about keratin tetramer composition

claim: Approximately 6 protofilaments are contained within a 10 nm keratin filament.
source: It has been previously shown that ~6 protofilaments are contained within a 10 nm keratin filament (Weber et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Weber et al., 2021

claim: The previously estimated keratin content in single basal keratinocytes of the murine epidermis is 8.07 ± 1.88 pg.
source: It is now possible to estimate the amount of keratin from our observations and to compare it to the previously estimated 8.07 ± 1.88 pg keratin in single basal keratinocytes of the murine epidermis (Feng et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Feng et al., 2013

claim: TSOAX provides density information of the identified keratin filaments.
source: TSOAX also provides density information of the identified keratin filaments.
evidence: Stated as a capability of the TSOAX software

claim: The generated TSOAX snakes are not separated consistently at filament nodes.
source: However, the association of nodes and segments is not detected satisfactorily as the generated TSOAX snakes are not separated consistently at filament nodes and therefore hinder statistical analysis.
evidence: Observed limitation of TSOAX output

claim: KerNet software was developed for optimal network representation of a node-segment structure.
source: We therefore developed additional tools (KerNet) for optimal network representation of a node-segment structure.
evidence: Stated as a contribution of this work

claim: The combination of TSOAX and KerNet analysis tools helped to create accurate numerical representations of keratin network topology.
source: The combination of the established segmentation algorithms (TSOAX) and the additional KerNet analysis tools helped to create accurate numerical representations of keratin network topology.
evidence: Stated as a result of the methodological approach

claim: Immersive environments improve the domain scientists' spatial judgment and task performance during visual analysis.
source: The benefits of such immersive environments have been demonstrated (Cruz-Neira et al., 1993; Laha et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cruz-Neira et al., 1993 and Laha et al., 2013

claim: An enlarged field of regard compared to standard desktop systems reduces clutter during data exploration.
source: Three factors thereby improve the domain scientists' spatial judgment and thus the task performance during the visual analysis: (i) an enlarged field of regard compared to standard desktop systems reduces clutter during data exploration, (ii) stereoscopy provides supporting depth cues, and (iii) head tracking provides enhanced motion parallax.
evidence: Stated as a benefit of immersive visualization

claim: Stereoscopy provides supporting depth cues in immersive visualization.
source: Three factors thereby improve the domain scientists' spatial judgment and thus the task performance during the visual analysis: (i) an enlarged field of regard compared to standard desktop systems reduces clutter during data exploration, (ii) stereoscopy provides supporting depth cues, and (iii) head tracking provides enhanced motion parallax.
evidence: Stated as a benefit of immersive visualization

claim: Head tracking provides enhanced motion parallax in immersive visualization.
source: Three factors thereby improve the domain scientists' spatial judgment and thus the task performance during the visual analysis: (i) an enlarged field of regard compared to standard desktop systems reduces clutter during data exploration, (ii) stereoscopy provides supporting depth cues, and (iii) head tracking provides enhanced motion parallax.
evidence: Stated as a benefit of immersive visualization

claim: This work provides the first experimentally derived numerical 3D representations of entire keratin networks in eukaryotic cells.
source: With this work we provide, for the first time, experimentally derived numerical 3D representations of entire keratin networks in eukaryotic cells.
evidence: Stated as a primary contribution of the work

claim: Comprehensive quantitative information on entire cytoskeletal networks is missing for most components.
source: Comprehensive quantitative information on entire cytoskeletal networks, however, is missing for most components and, consequently, only little is known about the distribution, local composition, mesh size, orientation, and mechanical properties of cytoskeletal networks at the subcellular level.
evidence: Stated as a gap in current knowledge

claim: Useful tools are available for the segmentation and modeling of actin filaments and microtubules.
source: To date, useful tools are available for the segmentation and modeling of actin filaments and microtubules but comprehensive tools for the mapping of intermediate filament organization are still lacking.
evidence: Stated as current state of available tools

claim: Comprehensive tools for the mapping of intermediate filament organization are still lacking.
source: To date, useful tools are available for the segmentation and modeling of actin filaments and microtubules but comprehensive tools for the mapping of intermediate filament organization are still lacking.
evidence: Stated as a gap in available tools

claim: The cytoskeleton consists of filamentous polymers which assemble into microtubules, actin filaments, and intermediate filaments.
source: The cytoskeleton is a key determinant of the necessary spatial organization. It consists of filamentous polymers, which assemble into microtubules, actin filaments, and intermediate filaments.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about the cytoskeleton

claim: Cytoskeletal networks act as structural and mechanical connectors between extra- and intracellular forces.
source: In this way, they act as structural and mechanical connectors between extra- and intracellular forces.
evidence: Stated as a known function of cytoskeletal networks

claim: The participating structures and polypeptides have been referred to as the mechanobiome.
source: The participating structures and polypeptides have been referred to as the mechanobiome (Kothari et al., 2019; Parajón et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2014), which defines the mechanical setting of a cell.
evidence: Supported by citations defining the term mechanobiome
